# Campaign results {#sec-campaigns}

**Of five configurations scored under a ten-fold sampling-density skew on
DrivAerML, only the similarity-gauge ISLA keeps its accuracy (1.21x); the
input-matched unit-drive GeoTransolver degrades 9.5x, Transolver 3.9x, and
the two other ISLA configurations 12x and 19x. And on the one real transfer
setting, fine-tuning from DrivAerML on 20 fastback labels is worth 31% for
GeoTransolver and nothing for ISLA.** This chapter collects the verdicts of
the node-budget campaigns (@sec-nb-campaign) as they close; each section
states the question, the preregistered bar, the float32 readout and what it
changes. Campaigns A (data-draw variance), B (random poses), D (interior
carriers) and the conditioning and diversity parts of C are still training
and are absent here by design.

## Few-shot adaptation on the fastback shift (campaign C, T3) {#sec-campaigns-fewshot}

The DrivAerML → SHIFT-SUV fastback shift is the program's one real
transfer setting: both architectures fail zero-shot (@sec-controls), and
the only known repair was training on the full 794-case estate family
(0.11–0.13 on the 99 fastback validation cases). T3 asks the practical
question: given 20 labelled fastback cases, does a source-only DrivAerML
checkpoint adapt better than a model trained from scratch on the same 20
cases for the same 1,000 optimizer steps? The preregistered fine-tuning
rate was 1e-4 against 1e-3 for scratch; a sensitivity arm at the matched
rate 1e-3 was added, with its bars, after the first readout showed the
1e-4 fine-tune under-adapted (@sec-nb-campc-t3, @sec-nb-campc-t3-verdict).

```{python}
#| output: asis
import json
from pathlib import Path
d = json.loads(Path("studies/campaign_c_transfer/campaign_c_t3_2026-09-10.json").read_text())["arms"]
rows = [("ISLA, fine-tuned from the DrivAerML reference, lr 1e-4 (preregistered)", "ft20_isla"),
        ("ISLA, fine-tuned, lr 1e-3 (matched to scratch)", "ft20lr3_isla"),
        ("ISLA, from scratch on the 20 cases, lr 1e-3", "scratch20_isla"),
        ("GeoTransolver (unit drive), fine-tuned, lr 1e-4 (preregistered)", "ft20_gt"),
        ("GeoTransolver, fine-tuned, lr 1e-3 (matched to scratch)", "ft20lr3_gt"),
        ("GeoTransolver, from scratch on the 20 cases, lr 1e-3", "scratch20_gt")]
print("| arm | seeds | fastback pressure | fastback wall shear | drag-coefficient relative MAE |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|")
for n, k in rows:
    a = d[k]; f = a["fastback"]
    print(f"| {n} | {a['n_seeds']} | {f['pressure_l2']:.3f} | {f['wss_l2']:.3f} | {f['CD_rel_mae']:.3f} |")
print()
print(": Relative L2 on the 99 SHIFT-SUV fastback validation cases (never used for adaptation), float32 inference, seed means over two fine-tuning seeds; every arm trains 1,000 optimizer steps at batch four on the same 20 cases. The drag coefficient is the recipe's integrated surface traction, mean absolute error over the reference mean (0.75). Data: studies/campaign_c_transfer/campaign_c_t3_2026-09-10.json. {#tbl-campaigns-fewshot}")
```

At the matched learning rate the two architectures separate cleanly.
GeoTransolver's DrivAerML pretraining is worth 31% (0.128 fine-tuned
against 0.186 from scratch), and the adapted model reaches the level the
program had only reached by retraining on 1,229 mixed cases, from 20 + 10
labels in about five minutes on one node. ISLA's pretraining is worth
nothing: 0.187 fine-tuned against 0.198 from scratch, inside the 5%
"worth nothing" clause of the sensitivity arm's bars up to rounding. The
scratch arms agree (0.19–0.20), so the architectures learn the same amount
from the target data and differ only in what they carry over from
DrivAerML. The preregistered "credible fallback" bar (≤ 0.15 and ≥ 2x
over scratch) is met by no arm, GeoTransolver passing the level and
missing the ratio; the preregistered 1e-4 fine-tunes were under-adapted
(ISLA 2.3x worse than scratch), which is why the sensitivity arm exists.

This is the third independent measurement in this program pointing the
same way: ISLA's zero-shot fastback force error of 1.6x
(@sec-controls-offset), the constant-gauge ISLA's collapse under density
skew (@sec-campaigns-density), and now a transfer value of zero for its
DrivAerML pretraining. What ISLA learns on DrivAerML is specific to
DrivAerML's conventions in a way GeoTransolver's representation is not,
and that is the concrete target for the architectural directions of this
program. Caveats: one source checkpoint per architecture and a two-point
learning-rate grid; a different rate or a warm-up could move either number
but not the sign of the difference at matched rate.

## Density robustness against fair baselines (campaign E) {#sec-campaigns-density}

The program book's remaining robustness claim for ISLA was that its
similarity gauge makes the prediction insensitive to how densely the
surface is sampled: on the 48 DrivAerML validation cars, a Poisson-biased
draw with ten times the inclusion probability on the front half of the car
(exact Horvitz–Thompson weights carried in the measure field, total measure
preserved) raised the gauge arm's pressure error only from 0.063 to 0.076,
a factor 1.20. The audit's objection was that no input-matched baseline had
been run through the same probe. Campaign E ran it, in float32 inference
(@sec-nb-campe-verdict for the preregistration and the bf16 preview), on
the canonical unit-drive GeoTransolver and Transolver checkpoints and on
three ISLA configurations.

```{python}
#| output: asis
import json
from pathlib import Path
d = json.loads(Path("studies/campaign_e_evalonly/campaign_e_density_fp32_2026-09-09.json").read_text())
b = json.loads(Path("studies/campaign_e_evalonly/campaign_e_density_bf16_2026-09-09.json").read_text())
names = {"gt_unit": "GeoTransolver, unit drive", "transolver_unit": "Transolver, unit drive (lr 3e-3)",
         "isla_reference": "ISLA, constant gauge (reference configuration)", "isla_gauge": "ISLA, similarity gauge",
         "isla_noweights": "ISLA, measure weights off"}
print("| arm | seeds | uniform draw | 10:1 biased draw | degradation factor (per seed) | bf16 uniform draw |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for k, n in names.items():
    a = d["arms"][k]; ab = b["arms"][k]
    seeds = ", ".join(f"{x:.2f}" for x in a["factor_seeds"])
    print(f"| {n} | {a['n_seeds']} | {a['unif_pressure_mean']:.4f} | {a['biased_pressure_mean']:.3f} | {a['factor_mean']:.2f} ({seeds}) | {ab['unif_pressure_mean']:.4f} |")
print()
print(": Surface-pressure relative L2 on the 48 DrivAerML validation cars, float32 inference, seed means; the factor is the biased-draw error divided by the uniform-draw error. The last column is the same uniform-draw evaluation in bf16, kept for the program's per-architecture offset table. Data: studies/campaign_e_evalonly/campaign_e_density_fp32_2026-09-09.json and campaign_e_density_bf16_2026-09-09.json. {#tbl-campaigns-density}")
```

The claim holds against fair baselines, by a wide margin: the
preregistered bar asked for a GeoTransolver factor of at least 1.32 with
the gauge arm's factor at most 1.24, and the readout is 9.5 against 1.21.
Every car is worse under the bias for every run of the four non-gauge arms.
The cost of the robustness is visible in the first column: the gauge arm is
10–20% less accurate on the uniform draw than the constant-gauge ISLA
(0.0558) and the unit-drive GeoTransolver (0.0505), so the trade is a fifth
of the accuracy on a well-sampled surface for an eight- to fifteen-fold
smaller error under the skew. The two non-gauge ISLA configurations are the
least robust of the five, and the weights-off configuration, which is the
program's best fair ISLA on canonical data (2.8% ahead of weights on),
reaches an error above 1.0 under the bias, worse than predicting zero. That
is the cost side of the weights-off decision: weights off is a canonical-
benchmark configuration, not a deployable one.

The mechanism, stated as the reading the numbers support rather than as a
separately tested result: the gauge normalizes ISLA's kernel by the local
measure, so the Horvitz–Thompson weights act as a quadrature correction and
the field is reconstructed from the sparse half nearly as well as from the
dense half; the constant-gauge ISLA meets weights far outside its training
range in every measure-weighted sum; the weights-off ISLA has no measure
and reads the front-heavy token cloud as geometry; GeoTransolver's
radius-based local features are neighbour statistics that shift ten-fold
with density; Transolver's learned slice routing degrades more gracefully.
A gauge arm with weights off would test whether the gauge alone suffices;
it is not scheduled.

One preregistration miscalibration is recorded rather than rewritten: the
"holds" clause named the ISLA reference configuration as the arm whose
factor had to stay within 1.24, but the book's 1.20 belongs to the gauge
arm, so the clause as written could not be met; the gauge arm is graded in
its place. A second, program-wide observation from the same evaluations:
bf16 inference inflates the uniform-draw error by 8.5–9.7% for
GeoTransolver and Transolver but only 2.8–4.0% for the three ISLA
configurations, so every bf16 comparison in the program has penalized the
baselines about 5% more than ISLA, which is one reason the program moved
to float32 as its reporting instrument.
